Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Aug. 29, 1919 County Superintendent of Public Schools Pierce County Tacoma, Washington My dear Mr. Cox: Mrs. Hattie Cowden, 612 South Tacoma Avenue, has applied for the discharge of Flora Porter, a [redacted] breed Eskimo girl, who was placed in this school seven years ago by Mrs. Cowden. Mrs. Cowden informs me that she is a teacher in the Tacoma schools and is acquainted with you. Before granting discharge to the girl, I would like some assurance that Mrs. Cowden is in a position to look after the girl's material welfare and is in other respects able to give a desirable home and protection to this girl. Thanking you in advance for any information you may be able to give me regarding Mrs. Cowden's financial standing and her character, I am Very truly yours, Superintendent. EHH:MC Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 10, 1919 Mrs. Hattie Cowden 612 So. Tacoma Ave. Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mrs. Cowden: The references received from the County Superintendent of Schools is satisfactory. I have a request from a respectable family in Seattle for a young girl. This request is in the shape of an offer to keep the young girl in school until she is through the 8th grade, and to pay her a weekly salary of $5.00. Flora tells me, however, that she does not wish to leave school if she can be enrolled in the Nursing course. I have no objection whatever to her leaving, except that I know Flora will have a much better future open to her on leaving Cushman #2 as a teacher or assistant nurse in the Alaskan School Service. Nevertheless, if you are willing to sign a contract to retain Flora in school until she has completed the 8th grade and to pay her $5.00 a week for her work out of school hours, you will have the preference in case Flora wishes to leave school. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 10, 1919 Mrs. Hattie Cowden 612 So. Tacoma Ave. Tacoma, Washington. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG Pierce County. Minnie D. Bean, County School Superintendent Agnes Streeter, Deputy Tacoma, Wash. Sept. 3, 1919 Mr. E. M. Hammond, Superintendent Cushman Indian School. My dear Mr. Hammond: Referring to your letter of August 29, will say Mrs. Hattie Cowden is reliable and a very good woman. I do not know of her financial standing. For information I refer you to Mr. Wm. M. Geiger of the city schools. B/R Very truly yours, Minnie D. Bean Co. School Supt. Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle *Excellent, good, fair, or poor. Sept 19th, 1919 Seattle, Wn. E. H. Hammond, Sup't. Cushman School. 2000nd. Wn. Dear Sir: We have been patiently awaiting to hear from you, concerning one of your pupils for Mrs. Schelthees. I received a letter yesterday from the Eskimo boy. It spoke to you about— He is very anxious to come out to school. Is it advisable for me to see Mr. Lopp? He is in Alaska at present. I will appreciate an early reply—as Mrs. Schuethes is very anxious to know. Very truly yours, Mrs. E. C. DeLou, 5215-19th W.E., Seattle, WA. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Oct. 10, 1919 Mrs. E. C. Decou 5215 - 19th N. E. Seattle, Wash. Dear Mrs. Decou: I am still unable to give you any definite information regarding a girl for your friend, Mrs. Schulthies. Mrs. Cowden who had applied for the services of Flora Porter is unable to give Flora the same terms you offered her, but insists that Flora should go with her and has taken the matter up with the Commissioner and as soon as he decides I will be in a position to state whether I can send Flora to you or to Mrs. Cowden. Respectfully, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Oct. 10, 1919 The Commissioner of Indian Affairs Washington, D.C. My dear Mr. Commissioner: Nine years ago Mrs. Hattie Cowden enrolled at Cushman School a [blacked-out] blood Eskimo girl, Flora Porter, an orphan, born 1902, for a term of five years, definitely surrendering any claims she might possess on the girl. At the close of the enrollment period Mrs. Cowden did not come for the girl. Two years later, last September, she came for Flora, stating that she needed her assistance in the house and agreed to keep Flora in school and to give her an occasional five dollars for clothing, etc, but of course could not pay her stated wages. I looked up Mrs. Cowden's references and found them satisfactory, but in the mean time a Mrs. DeCou of Seattle had applied for the girl, promising to keep the girl in school until she had finished the 8th grade and to pay her five dollars a week and her board. This offer was given to Mrs. Cowden who refused it as being most unsatisfactory and insisted on having Flora Porter turned over to her. This I am very much disinclined to do without explicit instructions from you as Flora is an orphan and I believe under the regulations, as representative of the Secretary of the Interior, I am her legal guardian. In two years time Flora will have completed the course at Cushman and will be in a position to obtain appointment in the Alaskan Teaching Service at $75.00 a month. Last June one of our Eskimo girls received appointment as Assistant Nurse in the Aklak, Alaska, hospital at $70.00 a month; and Flora can do the same which I think is a much better prospect for her than the one offered either by Mrs. Cowden or Mrs. DeCou. I am writing to you thus in detail as Mrs. Cowden advised me that she had taken the matter up with you. Respectfully, Superintendent. NURSING. I hereby certify that on May 26, 1919 (As soon after arrival as possible), I made a careful examination of the physical condition of Florence Porter, the child named in the foregoing application, and found her to be in proper physical condition to attend school. I therefore recommend that the said child be enrolled in this school. This 26th day of May, 1909 Blanche K. Turner, M.D. School Physician. INDORSEMENT. A child showing one-sixteenth or less Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, Indian fashion, who, if debarred from the Government schools, could not obtain an education, may be permitted in the reservation day and boarding schools, but it is preferable that it be not transferred to a nonreservation school, without special permission from the Office. Children showing one-eighth or less Indian blood, whose parents do not live on an Indian reservation, whose home is among white people where there are churches and schools, who are presumed to have adopted the white man's manners and customs, and are to all intents and purposes white people, are debarred from enrollment in the Government nonreservation and reservation schools. Superintendents, in all cases where doubt exists as to the degree of Indian blood of a child proposed for transfer, should fully satisfy themselves of the facts by affidavits from reliable persons, which affidavits must be kept on file at the school. A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both Superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and Superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. A pupil dismissed from school for cause must not be enrolled in any other school without the permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Full facts must be submitted with each request.
